parsed_answer.content:
Inheritance is a foundational pillar of Object-Oriented Programming (OOP) that enables code reuse, extensibility, and the establishment of an is-a hierarchy between classes. By allowing a subclass to inherit fields, methods, and behaviors from a superclass, developers can model hierarchical domain relationships and enforce polymorphic contracts via method overriding. However, despite its widespread adoption, inheritance introduces tight coupling, rigid hierarchies, and the fragile base class problem, making it a frequent source of technical debt when misapplied.

You should avoid inheritance when the relationship between your domain objects is not a true, strict is-a relationship, but rather a has-a relationship, or when you are simply reaching for inheritance as a convenient mechanism for code reuse. Relying on inheritance across deep class hierarchies means that internal changes to a superclass can inadvertently break subclass invariants, violating the Liskov Substitution Principle (LSP). Furthermore, modern software engineering favors composition over inheritance (as famously dictated by the Gang of Four), advocating for delegating responsibilities to collaborating components rather than binding behavior statically through subclassing.

rows: Tight (Subclass depends directly on superclass implementation details)
Static (Determined entirely at compile-time; cannot change behavior dynamically)
Dynamic (Behaviors can be swapped or injected at runtime)
High (Superclass modifications risk breaking hidden subclass logic)
Low (Encapsulated components protect clients from internal changes)

items: The Fragile Base Class Problem occurs when modifications to a superclass—such as adding a new method or altering internal method calls—silently break subclass functionality due to hidden assumptions about execution flow.

The Liskov Substitution Principle (LSP) mandates that objects of a superclass shall be replaceable with objects of its subclasses without altering the desirable properties of the program. Violating LSP via bad inheritance leads to runtime ClassCastExceptions or unexpected behavioral exceptions.

Deep inheritance hierarchies obscure the state machine of an object, forcing developers to navigate through multiple levels of overridden methods to understand a single execution path, severely degrading maintainability.

parsed_answer.content: Senior Engineer Trap: Never use inheritance solely for code sharing. If Class B wants to reuse a utility method or logging routine from Class A, use composition or static utility helpers instead. Once you expose a public or protected method via inheritance, you are locked into that API contract indefinitely, exposing internal state to subclasses and making refactoring exponentially harder.

title: What is inheritance, and when should you avoid it?
